lines.text: Bananas are berries in the botanical sense, but strawberries are not.
A sunflower's big head is made of hundreds of tiny flowers called florets.
Young sunflowers follow the sun across the sky. Grown-up ones mostly face east.
Bees can see ultraviolet light, which shows them hidden patterns on flowers.
Honeybees tell each other where flowers are with a little waggle dance.
Apples float in water because they're about a quarter air.
A strawberry wears its seeds on the outside, about 200 of them.
Earthworms have no lungs. They breathe through their skin.
Ladybirds love to eat aphids, which makes them a gardener's best friend.
Bamboo is a grass, and some kinds are among the fastest-growing plants on Earth.
Some bamboo can grow almost a metre in a single day.
You can tell a tree's age by counting the rings in its trunk.
Lavender belongs to the mint family.
Tomatoes are fruits, botanically speaking.
Peanuts aren't true nuts. They're legumes, like peas and beans.
Almonds are the seeds of a fruit that's a cousin of the peach.
Each cashew grows at the bottom of a fruit called a cashew apple.
A pineapple takes around two years to grow.
A pineapple is lots of little flowers that fused into one fruit.
A raspberry is made of many tiny drupelets, each with its own seed.
Coffee beans are the seeds of a small, cherry-like fruit.
Vanilla comes from the seed pods of an orchid.
Cacao pods grow straight out of the trunk of the cacao tree.
Avocados only start to ripen once they've been picked.
Banana plants are giant herbs, not trees.
Oak trees can live for hundreds of years.
A single oak can drop thousands of acorns in a good year.
Squirrels bury nuts and forget some, which helps new trees grow.
Dandelion seeds can drift a long way on the wind with their fluffy parachutes.
Clover and beans team up with soil bacteria to add nitrogen to the soil.
Moss has no roots. It holds on with tiny threads instead.
Ferns grow from spores, not seeds.
A mushroom is the fruit of a fungus that mostly lives hidden underground.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
Some fungi glow softly in the dark. People call it foxfire.
Fireflies make light with a chemical reaction that gives off very little heat.
Different kinds of fireflies flash in different patterns.
Frogs can soak up water through their skin.
Tadpoles breathe with gills before they grow lungs.
Butterflies taste with their feet.
Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres each year.
Hummingbirds can hover in one spot and even fly backwards.
Owls can turn their heads about 270 degrees.
Hedgehogs roll into a spiky ball when they feel scared.
Some snails can rest for months during dry weather, waiting for rain.
Bumblebees warm up by shivering, so they can fly on chilly days.
Many of the fruits we love need pollinators like bees to grow.
In Japan, cherry blossoms are called sakura.
Cherries, plums, peaches and apricots are all stone fruits.
Apples, pears, strawberries and roses all belong to the same plant family.
There are thousands of apple varieties around the world.
An apple seed rarely grows into the same kind of apple, so growers graft trees.
Pears ripen best after they've been picked.
Oranges and lemons are a special kind of berry.
Blueberries are native to North America.
Cranberries are often harvested by flooding the bog so the berries float up.
Fresh cranberries bounce, thanks to little pockets of air inside.
Some lotus seeds have sprouted after more than a thousand years.
Water rolls right off lotus leaves and carries the dust away with it.
Weeping willows love damp ground near ponds and rivers.
Cacti store water in their thick, juicy stems.
A cactus's spines are leaves that changed shape over time.
The saguaro cactus can live for well over a hundred years.
Some cactus flowers only open at night.
People have grown date palms for thousands of years.
Coconuts can float across the sea and sprout on faraway beaches.
A coconut isn't a true nut. It's a kind of stone fruit.
Mangoes are cousins of cashews and pistachios.
Edelweiss grows high in the mountains, wrapped in soft, woolly hairs.
Pine cones open up in dry weather and close when it's damp.
Most pine trees keep their needles all year round.
Coast redwoods are the tallest trees in the world, over 100 metres tall.
Some bristlecone pines are more than 4,000 years old.
Leaves turn yellow in autumn as their green fades and hidden colours show.
Red autumn leaves get their colour from pigments called anthocyanins.
Snowflakes almost always have six sides.
A layer of snow works like a cosy blanket for the soil underneath.
Rainbows appear when sunlight bends and bounces inside raindrops.
To see a rainbow, the sun has to be behind you.
The lovely smell of rain on dry ground is called petrichor.
Thunder is the sound of air rushing outwards from the heat of lightning.
Dew forms when cool night air turns water vapour into droplets.
Frost forms when water vapour freezes straight onto cold surfaces.
At the spring equinox, day and night are about the same length.
We have seasons because the Earth is tilted.
Plants breathe in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen as they make food.
Leaves have tiny pores called stomata that let air in and out.
Roots can sense gravity, so they know which way is down.
Seeds can wait quietly for years until the conditions are just right.
Some pine cones only open after the heat of a fire.
Every seed holds a tiny baby plant and a packed lunch of stored food.
Sunflower seeds sit in spirals that follow the Fibonacci numbers.
Pine cones and pineapples have spiral patterns too.
Compost is made by tiny creatures and microbes munching plant scraps.
A spoonful of healthy soil can hold millions of tiny living things.
Worms mix the soil and leave tunnels that let in air and water.
A layer of mulch keeps soil moist and cool.
Basil is a cousin of mint.
Rosemary, thyme and sage all belong to the mint family.
Mint spreads with underground runners, so many people grow it in pots.
A potato is a swollen underground stem called a tuber.
Carrots used to be purple or yellow. Orange ones came along later.
Peas climb by curling little tendrils around anything they can reach.
Ivy clings to walls with tiny roots along its stems.
Cut tulips keep growing a little in their vase.
Holly stays green and glossy right through winter.
European robins keep singing all through the winter.
Migrating birds find their way partly by the stars and the Earth's magnetism.
Ducks stay dry thanks to an oil they spread on their feathers.
Squirrels can turn their back feet around to climb down trees head first.
A rabbit's teeth never stop growing.
Sloths move so slowly that tiny algae can grow in their fur.
Geckos can climb glass thanks to millions of tiny hairs on their toes.
Spiders aren't insects. They have eight legs, not six.
Spider silk is amazingly strong for how light it is.
Dragonflies are expert fliers and can even fly backwards.
A snail's shell grows along with it its whole life.
The word daisy comes from 'day's eye', because it opens in the daylight.
Moonflowers open in the evening and close again by morning.
Many night flowers are pale, so moths can find them in the dark.
Bananas curve because they grow upwards, towards the light.
Watermelons are about 92 percent water.
A fig is really a cluster of tiny flowers, tucked inside out.
Some olive trees have lived for more than a thousand years.
Ginkgo trees have been around since the time of the dinosaurs.
It takes about 40 litres of maple sap to make one litre of syrup.
A honeybee makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its whole life.
Kiwi fruit grows on twisty climbing vines.
Lizards bask in the sun to warm up for the day.
